blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's critique of mainstream memory models (C++, Java) for their inability to support local reasoning due to unexpected behaviors arising from optimizations and relaxed memory models. The authors propose a novel memory model with 'local data-race-freedom' (local DRF), which bounds data races in both space and time, enabling programmers to reason about code fragments in isolation. The paper demonstrates surprising cases where seemingly race-free code can exhibit data races due to compiler optimizations or reordering, violating intuitive expectations. The proposed local DRF property ensures that accesses to a variable are unaffected by races on other variables, past, or future races, aligning with programmer intuition and supporting compositional semantics.
paper_title: Bounding data races in space and time
paper_abstract: We propose a new semantics for shared-memory parallel programs that gives strong guarantees even in the presence of data races. Our local data race freedom property guarantees that all data-race-free portions of programs exhibit sequential semantics. We provide a straightforward operational semantics and an equivalent axiomatic model, and evaluate an implementation for the OCaml programming language. Our evaluation demonstrates that it is possible to balance a comprehensible memory model with a reasonable (no overhead on x86, ~0.6% on ARM) sequential performance trade-off in a mainstream programming language.
